panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial DWI/ADC MRI from a 3-year-11-month-old boy with DADA2 showing acute diffusion restriction in the left-paramedial midbrain, i.e., a deep small-vessel ischemic infarct. The caption explicitly attributes these ischemic strokes to DADA2 (early-onset, recurrent, deep in the brain), and the article is a DADA2 cohort study, so disease attribution is direct. B: Axial T2 MRI from the same 3-year-11-month-old DADA2 patient showing two prior thalamic lacunar infarcts. Recurrent deep small-vessel strokes are a classic DADA2 presentation, and the caption explicitly ties these strokes to DADA2 in a DADA2 cohort article.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: H&E skin biopsy from a DADA2 patient (per figure caption and DADA2 cohort article) showing medium-vessel lymphovascular occlusion with neutrophilic infiltrate and intravascular thrombi, matching the configured necrotizing small- to medium-vessel vasculitis finding. Arrows annotate affected vessels. B: H&E section of a medium-sized artery from a DADA2 patient (caption: vasculitis in DADA2 patients resembling polyarteritis nodosa) with dense transmural mononuclear and neutrophilic infiltrate, karyorrhexis, luminal fibrin and vessel wall destruction — necrotizing medium-vessel vasculitis per the configured vocabulary. C: H&E section showing vasculitis of smaller vessels in the superficial subcutis; the biopsy was morphologically interpreted as possible polyarteritis nodosa, but the figure caption and DADA2 cohort article frame it as vasculitis in DADA2 patients (DADA2 vasculitis classically mimics PAN), so the panel is attributed to DADA2...

panels.figure_caption: The medium vessel vasculitis in DADA2 patients resembles the vasculitis in polyarteritis nodosa. (A) Sections of skin biopsy showing lymphovascular occlusion in medium vessels in the medium-to-deep dermis with inflammatory infiltrate with neutrophils and intravascular thrombi. (B) Vasculitis of a medium sized artery characterized by dense transmural infiltrate of mononuclear cells and neutrophils with karyorrhexis, fibrin deposits in vascular lumen, destruction of vessel walls and dense chronic inflammation surrounding the affected blood vessel. (C) Vasculitis involving smaller blood vessels of the superficial subcutis. This biopsy was interpreted as possible polyarteritis nodosa.

(a) Native T2-weighted; (b) Native fat-saturated T1-weighted; Gd-enhanced fat-saturated T1-weighted in the arterial (c) and late (d) phases. Multiple hyperenhancing focal lesions are visible in the arterial phase (arrows, asterisks), most are isointense on T2w and native T1w images, iso- or hyperintense in the late phase, with no washout. The lesions are relatively similar in size (10 to 25 mm) and imaging features. Two of the lesions (asterisks) are slightly hyperintense on T2w and hypointense on native T1w, while still enhancing after Gd injection.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial non-contrast head CT of a real pediatric patient from a disease-focused article ('Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage in Pediatric DADA2'), with captioned diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage of the basal cisterns (arrow). SAH is a rare, atypical CNS manifestation of DADA2 rather than a classic finding, so confidence is moderate; attribution rests on the disease-focused case-report title plus the captioned finding. B: Sagittal non-contrast head CT of the same pediatric DADA2 patient showing captioned subarachnoid hemorrhage in the posterior fossa (arrow). Same reasoning as panel A: real patient imaging tied to a DADA2-focused case report, but SAH is an atypical manifestation for the disease.
panels.attribution_text: Becker et al. Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage in Pediatric DADA2: A Case Report and Literature Review.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.106332. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Initial non-contrast computed tomography imaging Axial (A) and sagittal (B) non-contrast head computed tomography imaging demonstrating diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage, with predominant involvement of the basal cisterns in (A) and the posterior fossa in (B) (arrows).
in_text_mentions: Initial non-contrast head CT (Figure 2) demonstrated diffuse SAH, predominantly involving the basal cisterns and posterior fossa, consistent with Fisher grade 4, reflecting a high subarachnoid blood burden with associated hydrocephalus. No intraparenchymal hematoma was identified. Subsequent CT angiography showed no evidence of vascular bleeding. After imaging, an external ventricular drain was then placed for acute hydrocephalus (opening intracranial pressure 18 mmHg), and blood pressure was managed to maintain adequate cerebral perfusion. Coagulation was optimized with intravenous prothrombi

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is a gadolinium-enhanced T1 brain MRI of the DADA2 patient showing a focal enhancing cortical lesion in the left temporal lobe (arrow), attributed to DADA2-related inflammatory CNS involvement in this DADA2 case report. The specific lesion finding (focal enhancing lesion) is not in the vocabulary, so it is recorded as a proposed finding. B: Panel B is a gadolinium-enhanced T1 brain MRI of the patient whose brainstem infarction was identified as ADA2 deficiency (article title), showing the paramedian brainstem/interpeduncular cistern lesion with nodular enhancement, confirmed as infarction — a classic DADA2 CNS manifestation.

panels.rationale: Human pediatric brain CT from a case report of novel ADA2 variants, showing deep gray-matter low-density lesions typical of the small-vessel ischemic CNS involvement of DADA2; article title and caption jointly support disease attribution. CT rather than MRI, but the finding corresponds to the vocabulary's lacunar/deep cerebral ischemic lesion key.

in_text_mentions: te (ESR) was 47 mm/h (normal range 0-20 mm/h). IgA 0.19 g/L (0.31–0.67 g/L), IgM 0.61 g/L (0.98–1.789 g/L) and C3 1.71 g/L (0.6–1.5 g/L) were abnormal. IgG and C4 were normal. Serum autoimmune antibodies and demyelinating related antibodies (including Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein-IgG and Aquaproin Protein-4-IgG) were negative. White blood cells, protein and glucose in cerebrospinal fluid were normal. Bone marrow morphologic examination was also normal. Brain computed tomography (CT) showed multiple spotty and patchy low-density lesions in bilateral basal ganglia and thalamus (Figure 1).
